snippet.title: William Wallace’s Execution Was Worse Than Think
snippet.description: Join us as we strip away the Hollywood glamor and expose the harrowing, historically accurate reality of how Scotland’s greatest national hero actually died. We all remember the cinematic climax of Braveheart, where Mel Gibson defiantly screams "Freedom!" before a dramatic axe falls. But the real medieval punishment of being "hanged, drawn, and quartered" was infinitely more sadistic, calculated, and prolonged than anything shown on the silver screen. In this video, we trace Wallace's final hours on August 23, 1305, from his mock trial at Westminster Hall to the execution grounds at Smithfield. We break down the agonizing details of his four-mile journey dragged naked behind horses, the horrific process of being strangled nearly to death only to be cut down conscious, and the systematic public evisceration that followed. Discover how King Edward I used state-sanctioned terror not just to kill a man, but to completely dismantle a symbol of resistance—and why it ultimately backfired, cementing Wallace as an immortal martyr. Hit play to uncover the brutal truth behind the legend.

snippet.title: What Anglo-Saxon London Really Looked Like (AI Reconstruction)
snippet.description:
Forget the soaring stone of the Normans and the glass spires of the modern Square Mile. Before the Conqueror, there was Lundenburh.

Step back over a thousand years to a city of timber and tide, where the ghosts of Roman Londinium provided the bones for a resilient new world. In this immersive reconstruction, we peel back the layers of history to reveal a London defined by the scent of woodsmoke, the rhythmic tolling of bronze bells, and the relentless hustle of the Thames.

From the muddy wharves where global trade was born to the smoky hearths of wattle-and-daub homes, this is the story of a city that refused to die. Explore the fortified "burh" of Alfred the Great—a sanctuary of narrow, winding streets, vibrant markets, and the soaring timber heights of the original St Paul’s.

This isn't just a map of ruins; it’s a living, breathing look at the ambitious merchants, iron-willed women, and stubborn survivors who built the foundation of the world’s greatest metropolis.

This is London, stripped of its modern skin. This is the Anglo-Saxon soul of the city.

snippet.title: What Jerusalem Actually Looked Like Before Rome Destroyed It (AI Reconstruction)
snippet.description:
Basically, in this video, we bring Jerusalem back to life at its absolute peak, mere moments before it was consumed by fire and lost to time. It’s not just about looking at buildings; we explore the massive 36-acre Temple Mount that Herod the Great built , walking through the bustling Court of the Gentiles , and contrasting the palatial mansions of the Upper City with the crowded, noisy streets of the Lower City.

We also break down the exact events that led to the city's tragic fate, from the rise of early extremist factions like the Sicarii to the catastrophic siege by Roman forces in 70 AD. It’s crazy to see the historical irony of what was lost, and how Rome actually used the looted gold and enslaved population from Jerusalem's destruction to finance and build the Colosseum.

snippet.title: The Slave Rome Crucified For Public Entertainment
snippet.description: Join us as we step inside the blood-soaked sands of the Roman amphitheater to uncover a terrifying truth that mainstream history often ignores: the staging of fatal charades. While we frequently associate the Colosseum with gladiator battles or wild beast hunts, Roman emperors engineered an even darker form of mass entertainment—the public crucifixion of slaves disguised as grand mythological plays. In this video, we trace the heartbreaking reality of these state-sanctioned spectacles, where enslaved criminals and rebels were forced to play the roles of doomed mythical heroes like Laureolus or Prometheus. We break down the twisted mechanics of how a punishment designed for slow, isolated agony was turned into a theatrical performance for tens of thousands of cheering citizens, complete with elaborate stage scenery and special effects. Hit play to discover how Rome weaponized the human body to turn absolute cruelty into everyday public amusement.

snippet.title: Medieval London 1348 | A Day in the Life of an Alderman (Black Death) | Day 5 of 7
snippet.description:
In November 1348, three of London's twenty-four aldermen were already dead. Two more were sick. The constables who walked the streets were dying. The clerks who kept the records were dying.

And somebody still had to run the city.

This is Day 5 of our 7-part series: A Week in Medieval London.

Today, you are the alderman of Vintry ward — a wine merchant turned city official who has spent nine years managing eight thousand people on the north bank of the Thames. You know every street, every landlord, every problem.

This morning your ledger has three complaints waiting. One of them is a landlord refusing to let the collection carts remove the bodies of his dead tenants. You walk there yourself. He tells you: what's the point — they're all going to die anyway. You tell him: the point is that we do the work while we can. The bodies are collected.

At noon you walk to the Guildhall. Eight empty chairs where aldermen used to sit. The Lord Mayor is still in his. The agenda: the burial ground is running over budget, seven ward constables are dead and need replacing, and the city's finances are collapsing because the port is emptying and the merchants are dying. Nobody has a solution. The meeting ends anyway.

This afternoon you sit in judgment in the ward court. A weaver hasn't paid his rent. Both his journeymen are dead. His apprentice ran home. He chose food over rent. The law says evict him. You grant him thirty days.

Your wife says it best, over supper: he's not wrong that they're all going to die. He's just wrong that it matters.

Day 2 — The Monk
Day 3 — The Silk Woman
Day 4 — The Gravedigger
Day 5 — The Alderman (you are here)
Day 6 — The Physician

At noon you walk to the Guildhall. Eight empty chairs where aldermen used to sit. The Lord Mayor is still in his. The agenda: the burial ground is running over budget, seven ward constables are dead and need replacing, and the city's finances are collapsing because the port is emptying and the merchants are dying. Nobody has a solution. The meeting ends anyway.

This afternoon you sit in judgment in the ward court. A weaver hasn't paid his rent. Both his journeymen are dead. His apprentice ran home. He chose food over rent. The law says evict him. You grant him thirty days.

Your wife says it best, over supper: he's not wrong that they're all going to die. He's just wrong that it matters.

snippet.title: What Medieval London Looked Like 6 Weeks Into the Black Death | A Week in 1348 (Day 7 — Finale)
snippet.description:
December 1348. Six weeks after the Black Death reached London, the city is still standing — but it has lost as much as half its people. This is the finale of A Week in Medieval London: seven days, seven lives, one city.

Not the kings and cathedrals — the apprentice running a workshop he wasn't ready for, the monk singing the office with seventeen empty choir stalls, the silk woman reopening her doors, the gravedigger at East Smithfield who stopped counting at two hundred, the alderman who keeps showing up, and the physician who keeps writing it all down.

We step back from the six lives we followed all week and look at the whole city — what life was really like in medieval London during the plague, what the city lost, what it kept, and why London is still here almost seven centuries later.

This is Day 7. And today, you are a survivor.
